name: Barbell Clean
instructions: Start with the bar on the floor, feet hip-width, gripping just outside the legs.
Pull the bar explosively from the floor, extending the hips and knees, then shrug and pull under the bar.
Catch the bar in a front rack position in a full squat, then stand up to complete the lift.
coachNote: This is a highly technical lift requiring years to master — coaching from a qualified weightlifting coach is strongly recommended before loading heavy.
tips: Keep the bar close to the body throughout the pull.
Fully extend the hips before pulling under the bar.
commonMistakes: Pulling with the arms too early instead of extending the hips first.
Catching the bar too far forward or backward, losing balance.
benefits: Builds explosive full-body power.
Develops coordination, speed, and strength simultaneously.
safetyNotes: Learn the technique with an empty bar or PVC pipe first.
Use a qualified coach when starting out.
startingPosition: Bar on the floor, feet hip-width, gripping the bar.
endingPosition: Standing tall, bar racked at the front shoulders.

name: Power Clean
instructions: Start with the bar on the floor, feet hip-width, gripping just outside the legs.
Pull the bar explosively from the floor, extending the hips and knees, then shrug and pull under the bar.
Catch the bar in a front rack position in a partial squat (above parallel), then stand up to complete the lift.
coachNote: Catching the bar higher than a full clean makes this slightly more accessible while still training the same explosive pulling pattern.
tips: Keep the bar close to the body throughout the pull.
Fully extend the hips before pulling under the bar.
commonMistakes: Pulling with the arms too early instead of extending the hips first.
Catching the bar in too deep a squat, turning it into a full clean.
benefits: Builds explosive full-body power.
More accessible entry point than a full squat clean.
safetyNotes: Learn the technique with an empty bar or PVC pipe first.
Use a qualified coach when starting out.
startingPosition: Bar on the floor, feet hip-width, gripping the bar.
endingPosition: Standing tall, bar racked at the front shoulders, caught in a partial squat.

name: Hang Power Clean
instructions: Start standing, holding the bar at mid-thigh with a slight knee bend (the 'hang' position).
Explosively extend the hips and knees, shrugging and pulling under the bar.
Catch the bar in a front rack position in a partial squat, then stand up to complete the lift.
coachNote: Starting from the hang removes the floor pull, making this a great teaching progression for the explosive second-pull phase of the clean.
tips: Keep the bar close to the thighs throughout the pull.
Fully extend the hips before pulling under the bar.
commonMistakes: Pulling with the arms too early instead of extending the hips first.
Starting the hang position too low, essentially performing a full clean.
benefits: Simpler teaching progression than a full clean.
Builds explosive hip power.
safetyNotes: Learn the technique with an empty bar first.
Use a qualified coach when starting out.
startingPosition: Standing, bar at mid-thigh, knees slightly bent.
endingPosition: Standing tall, bar racked at the front shoulders.

name: Barbell Snatch
instructions: Start with the bar on the floor, gripping very wide, feet hip-width.
Pull the bar explosively from the floor, extending the hips and knees, then pull under the bar into an overhead squat position.
Catch the bar locked out overhead in a full squat, then stand up to complete the lift.
coachNote: Considered one of the most technical lifts in all of strength training, requiring exceptional mobility, speed, and coordination.
tips: Use a wide grip to shorten the distance the bar must travel.
Keep the bar close to the body throughout the pull.
commonMistakes: Pressing the bar out at the top instead of catching it locked out.
Catching the bar with insufficient overhead mobility, causing instability.
benefits: Builds explosive full-body power and mobility.
Develops elite coordination and speed.
safetyNotes: Learn the technique with an empty bar or PVC pipe first.
Use a qualified coach when starting out.
startingPosition: Bar on the floor, wide grip, feet hip-width.
endingPosition: Standing tall, bar locked out overhead.

name: Power Snatch
instructions: Start with the bar on the floor, gripping very wide, feet hip-width.
Pull the bar explosively from the floor, extending the hips and knees, then pull under the bar into a partial squat.
Catch the bar locked out overhead in a partial squat (above parallel), then stand up to complete the lift.
coachNote: Catching higher than a full snatch reduces the mobility demand while still training the same explosive pulling pattern.
tips: Use a wide grip to shorten the distance the bar must travel.
Keep the bar close to the body throughout the pull.
commonMistakes: Pressing the bar out at the top instead of catching it locked out.
Catching too deep, turning it into a full snatch.
benefits: Builds explosive full-body power.
More accessible than a full squat snatch.
safetyNotes: Learn the technique with an empty bar first.
Use a qualified coach when starting out.
startingPosition: Bar on the floor, wide grip, feet hip-width.
endingPosition: Standing tall, bar locked out overhead, caught in a partial squat.

name: Hang Power Snatch
instructions: Start standing, holding the bar at mid-thigh with a wide grip and a slight knee bend.
Explosively extend the hips and knees, pulling the bar overhead.
Catch the bar locked out overhead in a partial squat, then stand up to complete the lift.
coachNote: Starting from the hang is a great teaching progression for the explosive pull phase of the snatch without the added complexity of the floor start.
tips: Keep the bar close to the thighs throughout the pull.
Fully extend the hips before pulling under the bar.
commonMistakes: Pressing the bar out at the top instead of catching it locked out.
Starting the hang too low, essentially performing a full snatch.
benefits: Simpler teaching progression than a full snatch.
Builds explosive hip power and overhead stability.
safetyNotes: Learn the technique with an empty bar first.
Use a qualified coach when starting out.
startingPosition: Standing, bar at mid-thigh, wide grip, knees slightly bent.
endingPosition: Standing tall, bar locked out overhead.

name: Clean and Jerk
instructions: Perform a clean to bring the bar to the front rack position, standing tall.
Dip slightly at the knees, then drive the bar overhead explosively while splitting or squatting the feet under the bar.
Stabilize the bar locked out overhead, then bring the feet together to stand tall and complete the lift.
coachNote: One of the two competitive Olympic weightlifting lifts, combining a clean with an explosive overhead jerk in a single sequence.
tips: Keep the dip for the jerk short and vertical.
Drive the bar up and get under it quickly.
commonMistakes: Dipping too deep or leaning forward before the jerk.
Pressing the bar out with the arms instead of driving with the legs.
benefits: Total-body power and strength development.
Trains coordination between lower and upper body explosiveness.
safetyNotes: Master the clean and the jerk separately before combining them.
Use a qualified coach when starting out.
startingPosition: Bar on the floor.
endingPosition: Standing tall, bar locked out overhead.

name: Push Press
instructions: Stand holding a barbell in the front rack position at your shoulders.
Dip slightly at the knees, then explosively drive up through the legs to launch the bar overhead.
Finish by pressing the arms to full lockout overhead, then lower the bar back to the shoulders.
coachNote: Using the legs to help drive the weight allows significantly heavier overhead loading than a strict press.
tips: Keep the dip short and vertical, avoid leaning forward.
Drive through the whole foot during the leg dip.
commonMistakes: Dipping too deep or leaning forward, turning it into a push jerk.
Relying entirely on the arms instead of using the leg drive.
benefits: Allows heavier overhead loading than a strict press.
Builds explosive total-body power.
safetyNotes: Use a rack to start the bar at shoulder height.
Keep the core braced throughout the drive.
startingPosition: Standing, bar racked at the shoulders.
endingPosition: Bar locked out overhead.

name: Push Jerk
instructions: Stand holding a barbell in the front rack position at your shoulders.
Dip slightly at the knees, then explosively drive the bar overhead while re-bending the knees to catch it in a quarter squat.
Stand up to full lockout to complete the lift.
coachNote: Re-dipping under the bar allows heavier loads to be moved overhead than a push press since the legs absorb the catch.
tips: Keep the dip short and vertical.
Re-bend the knees quickly to receive the bar overhead.
commonMistakes: Pressing the bar out with the arms instead of driving with the legs.
Not re-bending the knees to catch the bar, turning it into a push press.
benefits: Allows the heaviest overhead loading of the pressing family.
Builds explosive total-body power.
safetyNotes: Master the push press before progressing to the push jerk.
Use a qualified coach when starting out.
startingPosition: Standing, bar racked at the shoulders.
endingPosition: Bar locked out overhead, feet reset together.

name: Split Jerk
instructions: Stand holding a barbell in the front rack position at your shoulders.
Dip slightly at the knees, then explosively drive the bar overhead while splitting one foot forward and one back to catch it.
Stabilize the lockout, then bring the feet back together to stand tall.
coachNote: The split stance allows the deepest, most stable catch position of all jerk variations, favored by most competitive weightlifters.
tips: Keep the dip short and vertical.
Split the feet quickly and symmetrically to receive the bar.
commonMistakes: Splitting the feet too late or asymmetrically.
Leaning too far forward or backward in the split position.
benefits: Allows the heaviest and most stable overhead loading.
Standard technique in competitive weightlifting.
safetyNotes: Practice the split footwork without weight first.
Use a qualified coach when starting out.
startingPosition: Standing, bar racked at the shoulders.
endingPosition: Bar locked out overhead, one foot forward, one back.

name: Dumbbell Snatch (Single-Arm)
instructions: Stand with a dumbbell on the floor between your feet, hinging down to grip it with one hand.
Pull the dumbbell explosively upward close to the body, extending the hips and knees.
Punch the dumbbell overhead to full lockout as it reaches shoulder height, catching it in a slight squat before standing tall.
coachNote: A more accessible entry point into explosive pulling patterns than a barbell snatch, popular in functional fitness and conditioning circuits.
tips: Keep the dumbbell close to the body throughout the pull.
Punch the dumbbell up rather than pressing it overhead with the arm.
commonMistakes: Muscling the weight up with the arm instead of using hip extension.
Letting the dumbbell drift away from the body.
benefits: More accessible than a barbell snatch.
Builds explosive power and conditioning together.
safetyNotes: Start with a light dumbbell to learn the pattern.
Keep the core braced throughout.
startingPosition: Dumbbell on the floor, hinged down to grip it.
endingPosition: Dumbbell locked out overhead, standing tall.

name: Thruster (Barbell)
instructions: Stand holding a barbell in the front rack position at your shoulders.
Squat down until your thighs are at least parallel to the floor.
Drive up out of the squat and use that momentum to press the bar overhead to full lockout in one fluid motion.
coachNote: A brutal combination of a front squat and push press, extremely popular in functional fitness competitions for its total-body demand.
tips: Use the momentum from standing up to help drive the press.
Keep the core braced throughout the entire movement.
commonMistakes: Pausing between the squat and the press instead of one fluid motion.
Using too much weight, causing poor squat depth or press form.
benefits: Builds total-body strength, power, and conditioning simultaneously.
Extremely time-efficient full-body exercise.
safetyNotes: Master the front squat and push press separately first.
Use a moderate weight to maintain good form.
startingPosition: Standing, bar racked at the shoulders.
endingPosition: Bar locked out overhead, standing tall.

name: Kettlebell Thruster
instructions: Hold two kettlebells racked at your shoulders, standing tall.
Squat down until your thighs are at least parallel to the floor.
Drive up out of the squat and press the kettlebells overhead to full lockout in one fluid motion.
coachNote: A more accessible entry point into the thruster pattern than a barbell version, common in kettlebell-based conditioning circuits.
tips: Use the momentum from standing up to help drive the press.
Keep the core braced throughout the entire movement.
commonMistakes: Pausing between the squat and the press instead of one fluid motion.
Using too much weight before mastering the pattern.
benefits: Beginner-friendly total-body conditioning exercise.
Time-efficient combination of a squat and press.
safetyNotes: Master the goblet squat and kettlebell press separately first.
Use a moderate weight to maintain good form.
startingPosition: Standing, kettlebells racked at the shoulders.
endingPosition: Kettlebells locked out overhead, standing tall.

name: Man Maker
instructions: Start in a high plank position gripping two dumbbells, feet wide.
Perform a push-up, then row each dumbbell up to your ribs one at a time.
Jump your feet forward to your hands, then stand up and press both dumbbells overhead to complete one rep.
coachNote: One of the most demanding combination exercises available, hitting the chest, back, legs, shoulders, and core in a single continuous rep.
tips: Move through each phase with control rather than rushing.
Keep the core braced throughout the plank and row portions.
commonMistakes: Rushing through the push-up or rows with poor form.
Using dumbbells too heavy to complete all phases with control.
benefits: Extremely time-efficient total-body exercise.
Combines strength, power, and conditioning in one movement.
safetyNotes: Master each individual component (push-up, row, squat, press) first.
Use hex dumbbells for stability.
startingPosition: High plank, gripping dumbbells.
endingPosition: Standing tall, dumbbells pressed overhead.

name: Devil Press
instructions: Start standing over two dumbbells on the floor.
Drop down into a burpee, placing your hands on the dumbbells and kicking your feet back, then perform a push-up.
Jump your feet back to your hands, then stand up and swing the dumbbells overhead to full lockout in one continuous motion.
coachNote: A punishing combination of a burpee and a dumbbell snatch, hugely popular as a conditioning finisher in functional fitness training.
tips: Move through each phase with control rather than rushing.
Use the momentum from standing up to help swing the dumbbells overhead.
commonMistakes: Rushing through the burpee portion with poor form.
Using dumbbells too heavy to complete the overhead swing safely.
benefits: Extremely demanding total-body conditioning exercise.
Builds explosive power and cardiovascular endurance together.
safetyNotes: Master the burpee and dumbbell snatch separately first.
Use hex dumbbells for stability.
startingPosition: Standing over the dumbbells.
endingPosition: Standing tall, dumbbells swung overhead.

name: Squat to Overhead Press (Dumbbell)
instructions: Stand holding a dumbbell in each hand at your shoulders.
Squat down until your thighs are at least parallel to the floor.
Stand up from the squat, then press the dumbbells overhead to full lockout as a separate phase after standing.
coachNote: Unlike a thruster, this separates the squat and press into two distinct phases, making it more accessible for beginners.
tips: Complete the squat fully before beginning the press.
Keep the core braced throughout both phases.
commonMistakes: Rushing the squat before standing fully upright.
Using momentum from the legs to help the press, turning it into a thruster.
benefits: Beginner-friendly total-body combination exercise.
Efficient way to train legs and shoulders together.
safetyNotes: Master the squat and shoulder press separately first.
Use a moderate weight to maintain good form.
startingPosition: Standing, dumbbells at the shoulders.
endingPosition: Standing tall, dumbbells pressed overhead.

name: Deadlift to Row to Press
instructions: Stand holding a dumbbell in each hand, hinge down into a deadlift position.
From the bottom, row both dumbbells up to your ribs.
Stand all the way up from the deadlift, then press the dumbbells overhead to complete one rep.
coachNote: A three-in-one combination movement that trains the entire posterior chain, back, and shoulders in a single efficient sequence.
tips: Complete each phase fully and with control before moving to the next.
Keep the back flat throughout the deadlift and row phases.
commonMistakes: Rounding the back during the deadlift or row.
Rushing through the combination instead of controlling each phase.
benefits: Highly time-efficient total-body exercise.
Trains the posterior chain, back, and shoulders together.
safetyNotes: Master each individual component first.
Use a moderate weight to maintain good form throughout.
startingPosition: Standing, dumbbells held, hinged into a deadlift.
endingPosition: Standing tall, dumbbells pressed overhead.

name: Dumbbell Clean and Press
instructions: Stand holding a dumbbell in each hand at your sides, hinging slightly to start.
Pull the dumbbells up explosively, dropping under them to catch them racked at the shoulders (the clean).
Dip slightly and press the dumbbells overhead to full lockout to complete the rep.
coachNote: A more accessible entry into Olympic-style lifting patterns using dumbbells instead of a barbell, popular in functional fitness training.
tips: Keep the dumbbells close to the body during the pull.
Use a slight leg dip to help drive the press.
commonMistakes: Muscling the dumbbells up with the arms instead of using hip extension.
Catching the dumbbells too high or too low at the shoulders.
benefits: Builds explosive power and total-body coordination.
More accessible than a barbell clean and press.
safetyNotes: Start with light dumbbells to learn the pattern.
Keep the core braced throughout.
startingPosition: Standing, dumbbells at the sides, slight hinge.
endingPosition: Standing tall, dumbbells pressed overhead.

name: Renegade Row to Burpee
instructions: Start in a high plank position gripping two dumbbells, feet wide.
Row each dumbbell up to your ribs one at a time, keeping the hips stable.
Jump your feet forward to your hands, then stand up and jump, reaching overhead, to complete one rep.
coachNote: Combines an anti-rotation core exercise with a full-body conditioning movement in a single efficient sequence.
tips: Keep the hips square during the rows, resisting rotation.
Move through the transition to standing with control.
commonMistakes: Letting the hips rotate excessively during the rows.
Rushing the transition to standing, losing balance.
benefits: Combines core stability training with full-body conditioning.
Time-efficient combination movement.
safetyNotes: Master the renegade row and burpee separately first.
Use hex dumbbells for stability.
startingPosition: High plank, gripping dumbbells.
endingPosition: Standing tall, jumped with arms reaching overhead.

name: Single-Arm Kettlebell Clean and Jerk
instructions: Stand holding a kettlebell between your feet, hinge down to grip it with one hand.
Pull the kettlebell up explosively, dropping under it to catch it racked at the shoulder (the clean).
Dip slightly and drive the kettlebell overhead to full lockout to complete the jerk.
coachNote: A staple kettlebell sport and functional fitness movement, combining an explosive pull with an overhead drive in one fluid sequence.
tips: Keep the kettlebell close to the body during the clean pull.
Use a slight leg dip to help drive the jerk overhead.
commonMistakes: Banging the kettlebell into the wrist or forearm during the catch.
Muscling the weight up with the arm instead of using hip extension.
benefits: Builds explosive unilateral power.
Popular in kettlebell sport and functional fitness training.
safetyNotes: Start with a light kettlebell to learn the pattern.
Keep the core braced throughout.
startingPosition: Kettlebell on the floor, hinged down to grip it.
endingPosition: Kettlebell locked out overhead, standing tall.

name: Wall Ball Shot
instructions: Stand a couple feet from a wall, holding a medicine ball at your chest.
Squat down until your thighs are at least parallel to the floor.
Drive up out of the squat and throw the ball against a target on the wall, catching it on the rebound to repeat.
coachNote: A conditioning staple that combines a squat and a throw, popular in functional fitness workouts for building endurance under load.
tips: Use the momentum from standing up to help drive the throw.
Catch the ball with soft hands, absorbing it back into the next rep.
commonMistakes: Not squatting to full depth.
Throwing with the arms only instead of using the legs to drive power.
benefits: Time-efficient total-body conditioning exercise.
Combines strength and cardiovascular endurance.
safetyNotes: Use a target height appropriate to your ability.
Keep the core braced throughout.
startingPosition: Standing, ball held at the chest.
endingPosition: Ball thrown against the wall after squatting and standing.

name: Medicine Ball Clean
instructions: Stand over a medicine ball on the floor, hinging down to grip it with both hands.
Pull the ball up explosively, extending the hips and knees.
Catch the ball racked at the shoulders in a partial squat, then stand up to complete the lift.
coachNote: A soft, forgiving object makes this a safe, beginner-friendly way to teach the explosive triple-extension pulling pattern.
tips: Keep the ball close to the body throughout the pull.
Fully extend the hips before pulling under the ball.
commonMistakes: Pulling with the arms too early instead of extending the hips first.
Rounding the back during the initial pull.
benefits: Beginner-friendly introduction to explosive pulling patterns.
Low injury risk due to the soft medicine ball.
safetyNotes: Use a ball weight appropriate to your strength level.
Keep the back flat throughout the pull.
startingPosition: Ball on the floor, hinged down to grip it.
endingPosition: Ball racked at the shoulders, standing tall.

name: Kettlebell Clean
instructions: Stand holding a kettlebell between your feet, hinge down to grip it with one hand.
Pull the kettlebell up close to the body, extending the hips explosively.
Rotate the hand as the kettlebell reaches shoulder height, catching it in the rack position without banging the wrist.
coachNote: Mastering a smooth, quiet catch at the shoulder — avoiding banging the forearm — is the key technical challenge of this lift.
tips: Keep the kettlebell close to the body throughout the pull.
Let the wrist rotate naturally as the bell flips into the rack.
commonMistakes: Muscling the kettlebell up with the arm instead of the hips.
Letting the kettlebell bang hard into the wrist at the catch.
benefits: Builds explosive unilateral power.
Foundational movement for kettlebell sport and training.
safetyNotes: Start with a light kettlebell to learn the catch technique.
Keep the core braced throughout.
startingPosition: Kettlebell on the floor, hinged down to grip it.
endingPosition: Kettlebell racked at the shoulder.

name: Kettlebell Clean and Press
instructions: Stand holding a kettlebell between your feet, hinge down to grip it with one hand.
Pull the kettlebell up explosively, catching it racked at the shoulder (the clean).
Press the kettlebell overhead to full lockout, then lower it back to the shoulder or floor to complete a rep.
coachNote: A complete combination lift that builds explosive power and pressing strength together in a single continuous movement.
tips: Keep the kettlebell close to the body during the clean.
Brace the core hard before pressing overhead.
commonMistakes: Muscling the kettlebell up with the arm instead of the hips.
Leaning back excessively during the overhead press.
benefits: Combines explosive power and pressing strength.
Time-efficient total-body movement.
safetyNotes: Master the clean and the press separately first.
Start with a light kettlebell.
startingPosition: Kettlebell on the floor, hinged down to grip it.
endingPosition: Kettlebell locked out overhead.

name: Kettlebell Snatch
instructions: Stand holding a kettlebell between your feet, hinge down to grip it with one hand.
Pull the kettlebell up explosively in one continuous motion, extending the hips and pulling the bell close to the body.
Punch the kettlebell overhead to full lockout as it passes shoulder height, catching it in a stable position.
coachNote: The competitive kettlebell sport movement — the key skill is a smooth, painless transition of the bell around the wrist at the top.
tips: Keep the kettlebell close to the body throughout the pull.
Let the wrist rotate naturally to avoid banging the forearm.
commonMistakes: Letting the kettlebell swing away from the body during the pull.
Muscling the weight overhead with the arm instead of the hip drive.
benefits: Builds explosive unilateral power and grip endurance.
Highly efficient total-body conditioning movement.
safetyNotes: Start with a light kettlebell to learn the catch technique.
Keep the core braced throughout.
startingPosition: Kettlebell on the floor, hinged down to grip it.
endingPosition: Kettlebell locked out overhead, standing tall.

name: Kettlebell Swing to Snatch
instructions: Perform a single-arm kettlebell swing, hinging at the hips and swinging the bell back between your legs.
Drive the hips forward explosively, using the swing's momentum to pull the bell higher than a normal swing.
Punch the kettlebell overhead into a snatch lockout as it reaches chest height, rather than letting it fall back down.
coachNote: Linking a swing directly into a snatch trains the transition between hip-driven momentum and the overhead punch in one fluid combination.
tips: Use the hip snap from the swing to help drive the bell upward.
Punch through at the top rather than muscling the arm overhead.
commonMistakes: Trying to snatch from a stationary position instead of using the swing's momentum.
Letting the kettlebell bang into the wrist at the top.
benefits: Builds explosive hip power translated into an overhead lockout.
Efficient conditioning and power combination.
safetyNotes: Master the kettlebell swing and snatch separately first.
Start with a light kettlebell.
startingPosition: Hinged forward, kettlebell swinging back between the legs.
endingPosition: Kettlebell locked out overhead.

name: Kettlebell Complex (Swing-Clean-Squat-Press)
instructions: Perform a kettlebell swing, then on the final rep, clean the bell up to the rack position.
From the rack, perform a goblet squat.
Stand up from the squat and press the kettlebell overhead to complete the full complex, then lower and repeat.
coachNote: Chaining multiple kettlebell movements into one continuous complex is a hallmark of efficient, high-intensity kettlebell conditioning.
tips: Move smoothly between each phase without setting the bell down.
Keep the core braced throughout the entire complex.
commonMistakes: Rushing between phases with poor technique.
Using a kettlebell too heavy to complete the full complex with good form.
benefits: Extremely time-efficient total-body conditioning tool.
Combines several fundamental kettlebell movements into one flow.
safetyNotes: Master each individual movement (swing, clean, squat, press) before combining them.
Use a moderate kettlebell weight.
startingPosition: Standing, kettlebell swinging.
endingPosition: Kettlebell locked out overhead after the squat.

name: Farmer's Carry
instructions: Stand holding a heavy dumbbell or kettlebell in each hand at your sides.
Walk forward for the desired distance, keeping the torso upright and shoulders back.
Set the weights down with control once the distance or time is complete.
coachNote: One of the simplest yet most effective total-body exercises — nearly every muscle works to keep the body upright and moving under load.
tips: Keep the shoulders back and chest up throughout the carry.
Take controlled, purposeful steps rather than rushing.
commonMistakes: Letting the shoulders round forward under the load.
Using a weight too heavy to maintain good posture.
benefits: Builds full-body strength, grip, and postural endurance.
Highly functional, carries over to daily life activities.
safetyNotes: Keep the core braced throughout the carry.
Choose a weight that allows maintaining upright posture.
startingPosition: Standing, weights held at the sides.
endingPosition: Walked forward while maintaining an upright posture.

name: Trap Bar Farmer's Carry
instructions: Load a trap bar and stand inside it, gripping the neutral handles.
Stand up tall and walk forward for the desired distance, keeping the torso upright.
Set the bar down with control once the distance or time is complete.
coachNote: Trap bars typically allow much heavier loading than dumbbells for this carry, making it a strong option once dumbbell weights are maxed out.
tips: Keep the shoulders back and chest up throughout the carry.
Take controlled, purposeful steps.
commonMistakes: Letting the shoulders round forward under heavy load.
Rushing the pickup, risking a rounded back.
benefits: Allows heavier total loading than dumbbells.
Builds significant grip and full-body strength.
safetyNotes: Deadlift the bar up with a flat back before walking.
Keep the core braced throughout.
startingPosition: Standing inside the loaded trap bar.
endingPosition: Walked forward while maintaining an upright posture.

name: Yoke Walk
instructions: Position yourself under a loaded yoke frame, standing tall with the frame resting across your upper back and shoulders.
Lift the yoke off its supports and walk forward for the desired distance, taking quick, controlled steps.
Return the yoke to its supports with control once the distance is complete.
coachNote: A signature strongman event that trains total-body bracing and stability under an extremely heavy compressive load.
tips: Take quick, choppy steps to maintain balance under the heavy load.
Keep the core and back braced hard throughout.
commonMistakes: Taking steps too large, risking loss of balance.
Rounding the back when lifting the yoke off its supports.
benefits: Builds extreme total-body strength and bracing capacity.
Classic strongman training tool.
safetyNotes: Use spotters when unloading or reloading the yoke.
Start with a moderate load to learn the walking technique.
startingPosition: Standing under the loaded yoke, frame across the back.
endingPosition: Walked forward while maintaining a braced, upright posture.

name: Zercher Carry
instructions: Hold a barbell in the crooks of your elbows, arms wrapped around it, standing tall.
Walk forward for the desired distance, keeping the torso upright and core braced.
Set the bar down with control once the distance or time is complete.
coachNote: The front-loaded Zercher position demands an exceptionally strong upright torso and core brace throughout the entire carry.
tips: Pad the bar or wear long sleeves to reduce discomfort on the elbows.
Keep the core braced hard throughout.
commonMistakes: Letting the torso collapse forward under the load.
Using too much weight before the elbow crease adapts.
benefits: Strong core and upper back demand alongside full-body carrying strength.
Unique loading position for training variety.
safetyNotes: Start light to adapt to the uncomfortable bar position.
Keep the core braced throughout.
startingPosition: Standing, bar held in the crooks of the elbows.
endingPosition: Walked forward while maintaining an upright posture.

name: Sandbag Bear Hug Carry
instructions: Lift a sandbag and hug it against your chest with both arms wrapped around it.
Walk forward for the desired distance, keeping the torso upright and core braced.
Set the sandbag down with control once the distance or time is complete.
coachNote: The shifting sand inside the bag adds an unstable load component that constantly challenges core bracing throughout the carry.
tips: Squeeze the bag tightly against the chest throughout.
Take controlled, even steps.
commonMistakes: Letting the bag shift excessively, causing loss of balance.
Rounding the back when lifting the bag.
benefits: Unstable load trains functional core bracing.
Highly practical, real-world carrying strength.
safetyNotes: Lift the bag with a flat back and braced core.
Start with a lighter bag to learn the carry.
startingPosition: Sandbag hugged against the chest.
endingPosition: Walked forward while maintaining an upright posture.

name: Sandbag Clean
instructions: Stand over a sandbag on the floor, hinging down to grip the handles or sides.
Pull the sandbag up explosively, extending the hips and knees.
Catch the bag racked against your chest and shoulders, then stand up to complete the lift.
coachNote: The awkward, shifting weight of a sandbag demands more total-body stabilization than an equivalent barbell clean.
tips: Keep the bag close to the body throughout the pull.
Use your legs to help absorb the catch at the chest.
commonMistakes: Rounding the back during the initial pull.
Pulling with the arms too early instead of extending the hips first.
benefits: Builds explosive power with a functional, unstable object.
Low-cost, versatile training tool.
safetyNotes: Use a bag weight appropriate to your strength level.
Keep the back flat throughout the pull.
startingPosition: Sandbag on the floor, hinged down to grip it.
endingPosition: Sandbag racked against the chest, standing tall.

name: Sandbag Shouldering
instructions: Stand over a sandbag on the floor, hinging down to grip both sides.
Pull the sandbag up explosively, using momentum to swing it up onto one shoulder.
Stand up tall with the bag on your shoulder, then lower it back to the floor and repeat, alternating shoulders.
coachNote: A classic strongman event that trains explosive full-body power in an asymmetrical, real-world loading pattern.
tips: Use the hips to generate power for the pull, not just the arms.
Rotate the bag naturally onto the shoulder as it rises.
commonMistakes: Rounding the back during the initial pull.
Using a bag too heavy to control the shouldering motion safely.
benefits: Builds explosive, asymmetrical full-body power.
Highly functional strongman-style training.
safetyNotes: Use a bag weight appropriate to your strength level.
Keep the back flat throughout the pull.
startingPosition: Sandbag on the floor, hinged down to grip it.
endingPosition: Sandbag resting on one shoulder, standing tall.

name: Sandbag Get-Up
instructions: Lie on the floor hugging a sandbag against your chest.
Use momentum and core strength to roll and stand up to your feet while keeping the bag held securely against your chest.
Once standing, reverse the motion with control to return to the lying position.
coachNote: A more accessible, less technical alternative to a Turkish get-up, since the bag stays hugged rather than locked out overhead.
tips: Keep the bag squeezed tightly against the chest throughout.
Use your legs and core together to help stand up.
commonMistakes: Losing grip on the bag during the transition.
Rushing the standing phase, losing balance.
benefits: Builds functional total-body strength and coordination.
More accessible than an overhead-loaded get-up.
safetyNotes: Start with a lighter bag to learn the pattern.
Move through each phase with control.
startingPosition: Lying on the floor, sandbag hugged to the chest.
endingPosition: Standing tall, sandbag still hugged to the chest.

name: Atlas Stone Lift
instructions: Squat down and hug a heavy stone (or stone-like implement) against your chest, tucking your hips underneath it.
Use a combination of leg drive and back extension to lift the stone up your thighs and onto your lap.
Stand up fully and lift the stone onto a platform, or simply to full lockout, to complete the lift.
coachNote: A signature strongman event requiring an unorthodox technique of scooping and rolling the stone against the body throughout the lift.
tips: Get as much of the stone against the body as possible before lifting.
Use the thighs as a resting point partway through the lift.
commonMistakes: Trying to lift with the back only instead of using the whole body to scoop.
Using a stone too heavy or slick to control safely.
benefits: Builds exceptional total-body strength.
Classic strongman training tool for raw pulling and lifting power.
safetyNotes: Use chalk to improve grip on the stone.
Start with a lighter stone or medicine ball to learn the technique.
startingPosition: Squatted down, stone hugged against the chest.
endingPosition: Standing tall, stone lifted to the chest or a platform.

name: Tire Flip
instructions: Squat down and grip the bottom edge of a large tire, positioning your body close to it.
Drive through your legs and back to lift the tire up, then push it forward to flip it over.
Reset your position on the other side and repeat for the desired number of flips.
coachNote: A high-intensity, explosive full-body movement that combines a deadlift-like pull with an explosive push, popular in strongman and functional fitness training.
tips: Keep the back flat during the initial pull phase.
Use the legs and hips to drive the push, not just the arms.
commonMistakes: Rounding the back during the pull.
Using a tire too heavy before building adequate strength.
benefits: Builds explosive total-body power.
High-intensity conditioning and strength combination.
safetyNotes: Use a tire size and weight appropriate to your strength level.
Ensure adequate space and a stable surface.
startingPosition: Squatted, gripping the bottom edge of the tire.
endingPosition: Tire flipped over to the other side.

name: Keg Carry
instructions: Lift a weighted keg (or similar odd, cylindrical object) and hold it against your chest, wrapping both arms around it.
Walk forward for the desired distance, keeping the torso upright and core braced.
Set the keg down with control once the distance is complete.
coachNote: Any shifting, liquid-filled, or odd-shaped object adds a unique unstable-load training stimulus not found with standard gym equipment.
tips: Squeeze the object tightly against the chest throughout.
Take controlled, even steps.
commonMistakes: Letting the object shift excessively, causing loss of balance.
Rounding the back when lifting the object.
benefits: Unstable load trains functional core bracing.
Builds practical, real-world carrying strength.
safetyNotes: Lift the object with a flat back and braced core.
Start with a lighter weight to learn the carry.
startingPosition: Object hugged against the chest.
endingPosition: Walked forward while maintaining an upright posture.

name: Sled Push
instructions: Stand behind a loaded sled, gripping the high or low handles with arms extended.
Drive forward by pushing through the legs in a low, powerful stance, taking quick, driving steps.
Continue for the desired distance, maintaining forward lean and drive throughout.
coachNote: One of the most joint-friendly ways to build leg power and conditioning since there's no eccentric loading phase.
tips: Keep a low, athletic stance with a forward lean into the sled.
Drive through the whole foot with each step.
commonMistakes: Standing too upright, reducing leg drive.
Taking choppy, ineffective steps instead of powerful drives.
benefits: Joint-friendly leg power and conditioning tool.
No eccentric loading, reducing muscle soreness risk.
safetyNotes: Ensure a clear, unobstructed path for pushing.
Start with a moderate load to learn the technique.
startingPosition: Behind the sled, low stance, arms extended to the handles.
endingPosition: Sled pushed forward for the set distance.

name: Sled Backward Drag
instructions: Attach a harness or straps to a loaded sled and face away from it, straps in hand or around the waist.
Walk backward, driving through the legs while keeping tension on the straps.
Continue for the desired distance, maintaining a controlled walking pace.
coachNote: This is a favorite knee-friendly quad exercise for rehab and prehab, providing significant quad loading with minimal joint stress.
tips: Keep the tension on the straps consistent throughout.
Take controlled, even steps.
commonMistakes: Walking too fast, losing tension and control.
Leaning too far back, reducing the quad demand.
benefits: Knee-friendly quad conditioning tool.
Popular for rehab and prehab programs.
safetyNotes: Ensure a clear, unobstructed path for walking backward.
Use a moderate load to start.
startingPosition: Facing away from the sled, straps in hand.
endingPosition: Walked backward for the set distance.

name: Sled Rope Pull (Standing)
instructions: Attach a rope to a loaded sled and stand facing it, holding the rope with both hands.
Pull the rope hand-over-hand, walking backward slightly with each pull to bring the sled toward you.
Continue until the sled reaches you, then reset and repeat.
coachNote: A full-body pulling conditioning tool that combines grip, back, and leg drive in a continuous hand-over-hand motion.
tips: Use your legs and body weight to help each pull, not just the arms.
Keep a steady, consistent pulling rhythm.
commonMistakes: Pulling with the arms only instead of using the legs and body weight.
Using a sled load too heavy to maintain a steady rhythm.
benefits: Builds full-body pulling strength and conditioning.
Complements sled pushing for balanced training.
safetyNotes: Ensure a clear, unobstructed path.
Use gloves if needed to protect the hands from the rope.
startingPosition: Standing, facing the sled, rope in hand.
endingPosition: Sled pulled all the way to the starting position.

name: Battle Rope Slams
instructions: Stand holding a rope end in each hand, anchored at the other end, in a quarter-squat athletic stance.
Raise both ropes overhead, then slam them down into the floor forcefully together.
Continue slamming for the desired duration, resetting your stance between reps.
coachNote: This is a highly effective, low-skill exercise for building explosive power and cardiovascular conditioning together.
tips: Use the whole body, including the hips and legs, to generate power for the slam.
Keep the core braced throughout.
commonMistakes: Using only the arms instead of engaging the whole body.
Rounding the back excessively during the slam.
benefits: Low-skill, high-intensity conditioning tool.
Builds explosive power and shoulder/core endurance.
safetyNotes: Use an appropriate rope thickness and anchor point.
Keep a stable, athletic stance throughout.
startingPosition: Quarter-squat stance, rope ends held, arms raised.
endingPosition: Ropes slammed down into the floor.

name: Battle Rope Alternating Waves
instructions: Stand holding a rope end in each hand, anchored at the other end, in a quarter-squat athletic stance.
Alternate raising and slamming each arm rapidly to create continuous waves traveling down the ropes.
Continue for the desired duration, maintaining a steady, athletic stance throughout.
coachNote: A staple cardio-strength hybrid exercise, excellent for high-intensity interval training with minimal skill requirements.
tips: Keep the stance low and stable throughout.
Maintain a fast, consistent rhythm with the arms.
commonMistakes: Standing too upright, reducing the core engagement.
Losing rhythm and consistency in the wave pattern.
benefits: Excellent cardiovascular and shoulder endurance builder.
Low-skill, accessible conditioning tool.
safetyNotes: Use an appropriate rope thickness and anchor point.
Keep a stable, athletic stance throughout.
startingPosition: Quarter-squat stance, rope ends held.
endingPosition: Same stance, arms alternating in a wave pattern.

name: Medicine Ball Slam
instructions: Stand holding a slam ball overhead with both hands, feet shoulder-width apart.
Forcefully slam the ball down into the floor in front of you, hinging at the hips and bending the knees as you follow through.
Pick the ball back up, resetting to standing, and repeat.
coachNote: An excellent stress-relieving, explosive exercise that trains full-body power output with a very low technical skill requirement.
tips: Use the whole body, including the hips and core, to generate power for the slam.
Fully extend overhead before each slam for maximum range.
commonMistakes: Using only the arms instead of engaging the whole body.
Rounding the back excessively when picking the ball back up.
benefits: Low-skill, high-intensity power and conditioning tool.
Great for reducing stress and building explosive output.
safetyNotes: Use a slam ball designed not to bounce back at you.
Keep the core braced throughout.
startingPosition: Standing, ball held overhead.
endingPosition: Ball slammed into the floor, torso hinged forward.

name: Medicine Ball Chest Pass Throw
instructions: Stand holding a medicine ball at your chest, facing a solid wall or a partner.
Explosively push the ball straight out from your chest toward the wall or partner.
Catch the rebound or the return pass, and repeat.
coachNote: This trains upper-body explosive power, useful for athletes needing fast pushing actions like offensive linemen or basketball players.
tips: Extend the arms fully and explosively on each throw.
Use a ball weight that allows a fast, powerful throw.
commonMistakes: Using a ball too heavy, slowing down the throw significantly.
Not fully extending the arms on the throw.
benefits: Builds explosive upper-body pushing power.
Highly transferable to sports requiring fast pushing actions.
safetyNotes: Use a solid wall or a partner positioned safely.
Warm up the shoulders before explosive throws.
startingPosition: Standing, ball held at the chest.
endingPosition: Ball thrown forward, arms fully extended.

name: Log Press
instructions: Clean a log implement (or heavily loaded barbell) up to the front rack position.
Dip slightly at the knees, then press the implement overhead using leg drive, similar to a push press.
Lock out fully overhead, then lower back to the shoulders with control.
coachNote: The neutral grip and thick diameter of a strongman log typically allow heavier overhead pressing than a standard barbell.
tips: Use the leg drive to help launch the weight overhead.
Keep the core braced throughout the press.
commonMistakes: Relying entirely on the arms instead of using leg drive.
Leaning back excessively during the lockout.
benefits: Allows heavier overhead pressing than a standard barbell.
Classic strongman competition lift.
safetyNotes: Master the push press with a standard barbell first.
Use a moderate weight to learn the log's unique grip.
startingPosition: Standing, implement racked at the shoulders.
endingPosition: Implement locked out overhead.

name: Burpee
instructions: Start standing, then squat down and place your hands on the floor.
Kick your feet back into a plank position, perform a push-up, then jump your feet back to your hands.
Explosively jump up, reaching your arms overhead, to complete one rep.
coachNote: The quintessential no-equipment conditioning exercise — simple to learn but extremely demanding when performed for volume or time.
tips: Move through each phase with control, especially when new to the exercise.
Land softly from the jump to protect the joints.
commonMistakes: Sagging the hips during the plank or push-up phase.
Rushing through the movement, sacrificing form for speed.
benefits: No equipment needed.
Extremely effective total-body conditioning exercise.
safetyNotes: Scale the push-up or jump if needed to protect the joints.
Land softly on the jump.
startingPosition: Standing.
endingPosition: Standing tall after the jump, arms overhead.

name: Burpee Box Jump Over
instructions: Perform a standard burpee facing a plyometric box.
Instead of jumping straight up, jump up and over the box, landing on the other side.
Turn around and repeat, alternating direction with each rep.
coachNote: A popular functional fitness competition movement that adds an extra coordination and power demand onto a standard burpee.
tips: Land softly on both sides of the box.
Use a box height appropriate to your jumping ability.
commonMistakes: Using a box too high before building adequate jumping capacity.
Landing stiffly, increasing injury risk.
benefits: More dynamic and engaging than a standard burpee.
Builds coordination alongside conditioning.
safetyNotes: Use a sturdy box and ensure clear space on both sides.
Master the standard burpee first.
startingPosition: Standing facing the box.
endingPosition: Landed on the opposite side of the box after jumping over.

name: Burpee Pull-Up
instructions: Perform a standard burpee positioned underneath a pull-up bar.
After jumping up, grab the bar and perform a strict or kipping pull-up.
Release the bar and land softly to complete one rep.
coachNote: Combining a push-dominant burpee with a pull-dominant pull-up creates one of the most balanced total-body conditioning movements available.
tips: Time the jump so you can smoothly grip the bar.
Use a kipping pull-up for speed if trained, or strict for strength focus.
commonMistakes: Mistiming the jump to the bar, wasting energy.
Sacrificing pull-up form for speed.
benefits: Balanced push-pull total-body conditioning.
Highly popular functional fitness competition movement.
safetyNotes: Ensure the pull-up bar is at an appropriate height and securely mounted.
Master both the burpee and pull-up separately first.
startingPosition: Standing under the pull-up bar.
endingPosition: Pull-up completed, then landed after releasing the bar.

name: Mountain Climber
instructions: Start in a high plank position with hands under the shoulders.
Drive one knee toward your chest, then quickly switch, driving the other knee in while extending the first leg back.
Continue alternating rapidly, as if running in place in the plank position.
coachNote: A versatile exercise that trains core stability and cardiovascular conditioning simultaneously with no equipment needed.
tips: Keep the hips level throughout, avoid piking up.
Keep the core braced throughout the entire movement.
commonMistakes: Piking the hips up into the air, reducing the core demand.
Letting the hands drift from under the shoulders.
benefits: No equipment needed.
Effective core and cardiovascular conditioning tool.
safetyNotes: Keep the wrists in a neutral position.
Slow down the pace if form begins to break down.
startingPosition: High plank position, hands under the shoulders.
endingPosition: Same position, knees driving in rapidly.

name: Bear Crawl
instructions: Get on all fours with hands under the shoulders and knees under the hips, lifting the knees an inch off the floor.
Crawl forward by moving the opposite hand and foot together, keeping the hips low and stable.
Continue crawling for the desired distance.
coachNote: A foundational animal-movement pattern that builds coordination between opposite limbs while training total-body stability.
tips: Keep the hips low and level throughout the crawl.
Move the opposite hand and foot together for a smooth pattern.
commonMistakes: Letting the hips rise too high.
Moving the same-side hand and foot together instead of opposite limbs.
benefits: No equipment needed.
Builds full-body coordination and stability.
safetyNotes: Use a pad under the hands and knees if needed.
Keep the core braced throughout.
startingPosition: On all fours, knees hovering just off the floor.
endingPosition: Crawled forward for the set distance.

name: Crab Walk
instructions: Sit on the floor with hands behind you, fingers pointing toward your feet, knees bent.
Lift your hips off the floor to form a tabletop position, then crawl forward or backward using your hands and feet.
Continue for the desired distance.
coachNote: This trains the posterior chain and triceps from an inverted orientation compared to a standard bear crawl.
tips: Keep the hips elevated throughout the entire crawl.
Move the opposite hand and foot together for a smooth pattern.
commonMistakes: Letting the hips drop toward the floor.
Moving too quickly, losing control and coordination.
benefits: No equipment needed.
Trains the posterior chain, triceps, and coordination together.
safetyNotes: Keep the wrists in a comfortable, neutral position.
Move at a controlled pace.
startingPosition: Seated, hands behind, hips lifted into a tabletop position.
endingPosition: Crawled forward or backward for the set distance.

name: Inchworm Walkout
instructions: Stand tall, then hinge forward and place your hands on the floor.
Walk your hands forward into a high plank position, keeping the legs as straight as possible.
Walk your feet forward to meet your hands, then stand back up to complete one rep.
coachNote: An excellent dynamic warm-up movement that combines a hamstring stretch with core and shoulder activation.
tips: Keep the legs as straight as comfortable throughout.
Take small, controlled steps with the hands and feet.
commonMistakes: Bending the knees excessively to compensate for tight hamstrings.
Letting the hips sag during the plank position.
benefits: No equipment needed.
Excellent dynamic warm-up for the entire posterior chain and shoulders.
safetyNotes: Move within a comfortable range of motion.
Bend the knees slightly if hamstring flexibility is limited.
startingPosition: Standing tall.
endingPosition: Standing tall after completing the walkout cycle.

name: Squat Thrust
instructions: Start standing, then squat down and place your hands on the floor.
Kick your feet back into a plank position, then immediately jump your feet back to your hands.
Stand back up to complete one rep.
coachNote: Essentially a burpee without the push-up and the final jump, making it a more accessible conditioning option for beginners.
tips: Move through each phase with control.
Keep the core braced during the plank portion.
commonMistakes: Sagging the hips during the plank phase.
Rushing through the movement, sacrificing form for speed.
benefits: No equipment needed.
More accessible entry point than a full burpee.
safetyNotes: Keep the movement controlled, especially when new to it.
Land softly when jumping the feet back.
startingPosition: Standing.
endingPosition: Standing tall after the thrust cycle.

name: Plank to Push-Up
instructions: Start in a forearm plank position, body in a straight line.
Push up one arm at a time to a high plank (push-up) position.
Lower back down one arm at a time to the forearm plank, alternating the leading arm each cycle.
coachNote: Also known as a plank walk-up, this combines an anti-rotation core challenge with shoulder and tricep endurance work.
tips: Keep the hips as still as possible throughout each transition.
Alternate the leading arm evenly.
commonMistakes: Letting the hips rock side to side during the transitions.
Rushing through the movement.
benefits: Combines core stability with upper body pushing endurance.
No equipment needed.
safetyNotes: Master a standard plank hold before adding transitions.
Keep the core braced throughout.
startingPosition: Forearm plank position.
endingPosition: High plank position after pushing up.

name: Prowler Sprint (Light Sled)
instructions: Stand behind a lightly loaded sled, gripping the high handles.
Sprint forward as quickly as possible while pushing the sled, maintaining a fast turnover of the legs.
Continue for the desired distance, then walk back to reset.
coachNote: Using a lighter load than a heavy sled push shifts the emphasis toward speed and cardiovascular conditioning rather than maximal strength.
tips: Focus on fast, driving steps rather than maximal force per step.
Keep a slight forward lean throughout the sprint.
commonMistakes: Loading the sled too heavy, turning it into a strength exercise instead of a speed one.
Standing too upright, reducing drive efficiency.
benefits: Builds speed and cardiovascular conditioning.
Low-impact alternative to traditional sprinting.
safetyNotes: Ensure a long, clear, unobstructed path.
Warm up thoroughly before sprinting efforts.
startingPosition: Behind the lightly loaded sled, hands on the handles.
endingPosition: Sled sprinted forward for the set distance.
